passage: In art class, Sir held up his own cow drawing, which looked a lot like a table. “Behold, my masterpiece!” he said, and the whole class laughed, including Sir. Later, when Chaitanya knocked over the water jar and it splashed across the floor, a few children laughed too. But Chaitanya didn't laugh. He stared at his shoes, his ears red. Pradeep felt the two kinds of laughter were not the same. The first had made Sir look happy. The second made Chaitanya look small. Pradeep didn't join in. He picked up a cloth and said, “I'll help.”

qa.q: What did Sir's cow drawing look like?
qa.a: It looked a lot like a table.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya probably feeling when the children laughed and he stared at his shoes, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and hurt, since his ears went red and he did not laugh. He might also have been worried about the mess.

qa.q: How did the two kinds of laughter differ, and what did Pradeep do?
qa.a: Sir laughed with everyone at a joke he made on himself, while some children laughed at Chaitanya's mistake. Pradeep did not join in and helped clean up instead.

qa.q: How might Sir see the first laughter?
qa.a: As friendly and shared, since he was laughing with the class. He might not have noticed the second kind if he was looking at the board.

grounding: Laughing with someone is friendly and includes them; laughing at someone's mistake can hurt.

passage: I'm Parveen. At assembly, Ujjwal read the notice in a funny cartoon voice, and the whole hall laughed. He grinned and bowed a bit. That was laughing with him, because he had made the joke. An hour later, during the races, his big borrowed shoe flew off and a few boys laughed. This time Ujjwal did not grin. He hopped over and looked at the ground. I wasn't sure what he felt, maybe embarrassed, maybe he was just annoyed. I picked up the shoe and said, “Here.” He said thanks, quietly, and we jogged back together.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal read in a cartoon voice?
qa.a: He read the notice in a cartoon voice at assembly.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal seem to feel about the two kinds of laughter, and how sure can Parveen be?
qa.a: He grinned at the first, which he had invited, and did not grin at the second, so he probably felt embarrassed by it. Parveen admits not being sure; he might also have been annoyed.

qa.q: What did Parveen do that was a good response to laughter at Ujjwal's mistake?
qa.a: Parveen did not join the laughing, picked up the shoe and offered it, then jogged back with Ujjwal.

qa.q: How might the boys who laughed see what happened?
qa.a: They might have thought it was just funny, not noticing Ujjwal did not enjoy it. Seeing Parveen help may make them think again.

grounding: Laughing with a person differs from laughing at a mistake; an observer notices and helps.

passage: Monday: Harish tripped over a bag in class and sprawled on the floor. Everyone laughed, and Sarita laughed loudest, pointing. Harish got up slowly, red-faced, and didn't look at anyone all morning. Sarita's stomach felt strange. Wednesday: At lunch Harish did an impression of his own trip, arms windmilling, with a dramatic “Nooo!” This time everyone laughed, Harish most of all, and he bowed. Sarita noticed the difference: he started it, he was grinning, he was in on it. Friday: When a boy mocked the new girl's lunch and a few kids snickered, Sarita didn't laugh. She moved her tiffin next to the new girl's.

qa.q: What did Harish trip over on Monday?
qa.a: Harish tripped over a bag in class.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when her stomach felt strange on Monday?
qa.a: Sarita felt guilty and uneasy, sensing her pointing laughter had hurt Harish.

qa.q: What did Sarita do on Friday, and why was it right?
qa.a: Sarita didn't join the snickering and sat with the new girl, refusing to laugh at someone's difference.

qa.q: What made Wednesday's laughter feel different for Harish?
qa.a: Harish started the joke himself, so he was laughing with everyone and felt included rather than mocked.

grounding: Shows a child learning to tell laughter that mocks a mistake from warm laughter that includes, and not joining in at another's expense.

passage: Swati, you ask how to tell if people are laughing with you. Let your Jatin Dadu tell you about the Ramlila when I was twelve. I played a monkey soldier, and my tail fell off in the middle of the battle. The whole crowd roared. Some boys at the front pointed and shouted, “Tail-less monkey!” and kept shouting long after the scene ended. But my friend Sohan, playing Hanuman, picked up the tail, waved it like a flag and bowed with me. The crowd cheered. Sohan's laugh had room for me in it; the boys' laugh pushed me out. That night, when one of those boys fell off his bicycle, I didn't laugh. I helped him up.

qa.q: What role did young Jatin play in the Ramlila?
qa.a: He played a monkey soldier.

qa.q: What was young Jatin feeling when the boys kept shouting “Tail-less monkey”?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and pushed out, unlike the moment Sohan turned the fall into a shared joke.

qa.q: What choice did Jatin make that night, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He helped the boy who fell off his bicycle instead of laughing, choosing not to repeat the mocking he had felt.

qa.q: How did Sohan's laughter feel different to the crowd?
qa.a: Sohan's waving and bowing invited the crowd to laugh with Jatin, so they cheered instead of jeering.

grounding: Shows a child telling friendly laughter that includes him from laughter that mocks, and choosing not to laugh at another's mishap.

passage: The school bus was crawling through traffic, the teacher was at the front on the phone, and the back seats were loud. When Maria sang a Konkani song her grandmother taught her, three boys copied the words in silly voices and hooted. Maria kept singing, but her voice got smaller. Rashmi, sitting across from them, felt a laugh bubble up. It was a funny sound. Then she saw Maria's hands gripping the seat and her eyes fixed on the window. This wasn't laughing with her. Rashmi clapped along to the tune instead. “Teach me the chorus?” Maria looked at her, surprised, and began again, louder.

qa.q: Who taught Maria the Konkani song?
qa.a: Her grandmother taught her the song.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as her voice got smaller?
qa.a: Maria felt hurt and embarrassed by the boys copying her in silly voices.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do instead of laughing, and why did it help?
qa.a: Rashmi clapped along and asked to learn the chorus, turning the moment from mockery into warm, shared fun.

qa.q: How might the boys see their hooting?
qa.a: They might think it was harmless fun, not seeing Maria's gripping hands and fixed eyes that showed hurt.

grounding: Shows a child noticing that laughter at a classmate's language is mocking, and choosing warm, inclusive laughter instead.

passage:
At skit practice in the school activity room in Chennai, Rekha tripped over her own dupatta and landed on a beanbag. She lay there giggling. "Graceful swan, that's me!" Everyone laughed, Rekha loudest.

Ten minutes later it was Shreya's line. "Mother, pass me the re-sipe book."

Someone snorted. Nitin copied her in a squeaky voice, "re-SIPE", and a few others laughed. Shreya didn't. Her ears went red, and she stared at her script.

Rekha felt the difference like a draught of cold air. The first laugh had been hers to share; this one was being done to Shreya. "It's a weird word," Rekha said. "I said it that way till Class 5. Go on, Shreya."

qa.q: What did Rekha trip over?
qa.a: Her own dupatta.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when her ears went red and she stared at her script?
qa.a: Embarrassed and hurt, because the others were laughing at her mistake, not with her.

qa.q: What did Rekha do to stop the mocking laughter?
qa.a: She didn't join in; she said it's a weird word, admitted she said it the same way till Class 5, and told Shreya to go on.

qa.q: How might Nitin see his squeaky copy?
qa.a: Nitin may think it was harmless fun, like the laugh at Rekha's fall, without noticing that Shreya wasn't laughing.

grounding: It shows a child telling shared laughter at her own fall from laughter that mocks a classmate's mistake, and refusing to join in.
